doi:10.1002/jcal.70366.detail: Researchers used chat logs, screen recordings and interviews to follow 411 moments in the writing task. As disagreement intensified, both higher- and lower-scoring writers sometimes moved from accepting or considering a suggestion to rejecting it.
doi:10.1002/jcal.70366.lead: While writing reports with AI, 21 students sometimes rejected suggestions after a disagreement. A rejection alone could mean the student had found a problem or was frustrated with the task.
doi:10.1002/jcal.70366.limit: The 411 observations came from repeated moments involving the same 21 writers. Each writer took part in one task.

doi:10.1002/jcal.70367.detail: The study also asks how students’ knowledge of AI relates to confidence, motivation, mental effort and the way they interact with the tool during writing.
doi:10.1002/jcal.70367.lead: The authors ask how students’ knowledge of AI relates to writing a research abstract with it. They distinguish knowing how the tool works from knowing how to use it and judge what it produces.
doi:10.1002/jcal.70367.limit: The available abstract cuts off during the methods. It gives the questions the researchers asked but does not establish how students performed.

doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02400-z.detail: The authors connect a platform’s interest in repeated visits with its ability to learn users’ habits from records of past behavior.
doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02400-z.lead: This paper asks how platforms make money by shaping what people notice. The authors argue that the design of a person’s digital surroundings matters for understanding how everyday habits develop.
doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02400-z.limit: This is an argument about business models and design. It does not estimate how much time any one platform takes from a user.

doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02405-8.detail: One of the authors’ design questions is whether a tool can help people notice the values behind decisions about what deserves attention.
doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02405-8.lead: This manifesto asks designers to consider what their tools help people pay attention to. The authors draw on Buddhist philosophy to make a case for technology that helps people notice and respond to others’ suffering.
doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02405-8.limit: The manifesto proposes questions for researchers and designers. It does not report a test of a particular design.

doi:10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6.detail: In the authors’ framework, a teacher identifies the reasoning a student should be able to explain and asks how the student would check AI’s work against evidence from the subject.
doi:10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6.lead: The authors propose a way to decide which parts of a science or math task students should do themselves. They suggest starting with the skill being taught and checking whether students can reconstruct the essential steps.
doi:10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6.limit: The authors have yet to test whether their proposed checks capture something beyond a student’s existing subject knowledge.

doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.detail: Thirty business students practiced with the chatbot. Its final case appeared 146 times and drew 91 answers. A student could open the tutor more than once.
doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.lead: Students opened a GPT practice exam 224 times. Only 118 of those sessions included an answer to the first question.
doi:10.1007/s11423-026-10749-1.limit: The class used Moodle for a different topic. Its logs counted attempts without showing which questions students answered, so the totals cannot tell us which tool taught more.

doi:10.1007/s42438-026-00721-w.detail: Students would inspect a plan for measuring an enzyme reaction. Asking why temperature matters could reveal which conditions they understand well enough to check themselves.
doi:10.1007/s42438-026-00721-w.lead: In a proposed biochemistry lesson, students inspect an AI-generated experiment and explain how they would check it. Spotting a missing control gives the teacher something to discuss with the student.
doi:10.1007/s42438-026-00721-w.limit: The authors describe a lesson a teacher could try. They have yet to observe students doing it.

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02808-6.detail: Someone reading about AI-assisted data analysis might check the code. Someone reading about AI-assisted proofreading might look for traces of the tool in the wording. Matsui suggests tracking what readers flag and remember.
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02808-6.lead: Would you read a paper differently if its authors used AI to edit the grammar or to analyze the data? Matsui proposes showing readers different disclosures on the same paper to see what they check.
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02808-6.limit: The paper describes how to test those possibilities. Readers’ actual responses remain unknown.

doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2023.100198.detail: Sixty students used ChatGPT and 65 used other tools. Both groups filled out questionnaires before and after the course activities, and they started with different average critical-thinking scores.
doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2023.100198.lead: In a research methods course in Ghana, students who used ChatGPT rated their critical, creative and reflective thinking higher after three weeks than classmates who used search tools. Those scores came from questionnaires.
doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2023.100198.limit: The paper gives conflicting accounts of how the groups were formed. It also leaves open whether students could evaluate a new claim on their own.

doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100571.detail: The reviewers describe assignments where students were prompted to question an answer or use criteria to judge it. They suggest such guidance as one option for teachers designing an activity.
doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100571.lead: A review of 67 studies found that how teachers structured ChatGPT assignments mattered. The reviewers report that tasks with guidance for evaluating answers often supported both generating ideas and judging them.
doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100571.limit: The review brings together different tasks. Its account cannot tell a teacher how much one prompt will help in a particular class.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386.detail: After 20 minutes of research, 91 students put away their sources and notes. Their recommendations included an average of 1.20 of seven relevant points with ChatGPT and 1.87 with Google.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386.lead: Students researched sunscreen ingredients using ChatGPT or Google, then wrote recommendations from memory. The ChatGPT group described the task as easier but included fewer relevant points on average.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386.limit: The exercise covered one sunscreen question. It leaves open whether either group would remember the evidence later or apply it to a different decision.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108779.detail: The researchers compared people working with AI, people working alone and the AI’s own answers. In the reported comparison, the AI-assisted group outscored the unassisted group on average.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108779.lead: People used AI to answer 20 logic questions from a law school admissions test. In one study, they scored higher than a reference group yet estimated their own scores about four points too high on average.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108779.limit: The test used a specific set of logic problems. It does not show whether confidence matches performance on other tasks.

doi:10.1016/j.chb.2026.109217.detail: Researchers distinguished having access to AI feedback from choosing to use it regularly. They compared students’ reports about the effort that went into understanding the game and the effort spent dealing with unnecessary demands.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2026.109217.lead: Over five weeks, students played a business simulation. Researchers tracked who used its AI feedback and asked students how mentally demanding the game felt.
doi:10.1016/j.chb.2026.109217.limit: People who chose to use the feedback could differ from those who left it alone. This comparison cannot isolate what the feedback itself changed.

doi:10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100378.detail: Researchers coded the prompts of 171 secondary and university students in 45 teams. As play progressed, teams shifted toward prompts about their own approach to the mystery.
doi:10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100378.lead: Students worked in teams to solve a mystery with AI. Teams that spent more of their prompts creating ideas or checking their thinking did better on the task, even after researchers accounted for how many prompts they sent.
doi:10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100378.limit: Students formed their own teams and chose their prompts. The link with success cannot show that a particular prompt made a team better.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101103.detail: Across six studies, researchers also checked whether people got similar scores when they took the questionnaire again. The fact-checking exercise gave them a separate way to test what the scores meant.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101103.lead: Researchers asked people how they checked AI answers, then gave them a chatbot fact-checking task. People who scored higher on the questionnaire also judged the answers more accurately.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101103.limit: The samples consisted of English-speaking online participants and university students. The scale needs checking in other languages and settings.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101130.detail: Researchers coded 281 prompts in 122 assignment submissions, looking at which features tended to occur together, such as giving an instruction and adding context.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101130.lead: Students used AI to build datasets about social networks. In higher-rated assignments, students more often told the tool both what to do and what background it needed.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101130.limit: Prompt text leaves out the thinking that happened before a student typed. The comparison cannot show that one style of prompting improved learning.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101340.detail: In a Finnish methods course, students could use AI on a home exam if they explained how. Researchers compared those accounts with exam answers and marks for 891 students.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101340.lead: In take-home exams, students who described checking and revising AI suggestions tended to earn stronger marks. Some students who relied on generic AI answers missed what the course required in a definition.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101340.limit: Students described their own use in varying detail. Researchers lacked the prompts needed to check exactly what each student asked.

doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101420.detail: At the first survey, 1,025 medical students answered questions about their phone habits. Of those, 65% completed all three surveys, which let researchers compare their answers over time.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101420.lead: Researchers followed 668 medical students across eight months. Students answered questions about habits such as worrying and about their use of smartphone apps.
doi:10.1016/j.chbr.2026.101420.limit: The study relied on students’ reports of their app use, without phone logs to check them. People who left the study may have had different habits.

doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106458.detail: The experiments mixed trials where only one task was available with trials where participants could decide what to do. Researchers separately tracked the time a switch took and how often people chose it.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106458.lead: In two experiments, people who had recently switched tasks lost less time on their next switch. When given a choice, they were also more likely to switch again.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106458.limit: The pattern carried over clearly to a new pair of tasks in only one of the two experiments that tested that question.

doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104977.detail: Four students wrote essays and four designed slides on the same subject. Researchers recorded their screens, listened as they talked through choices and later interviewed them about their work.
doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104977.lead: Students making slides used one AI tool to describe a picture and another to generate it. Researchers followed how the students judged and refined the images they put in their presentations.
doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104977.limit: Eight volunteers at one university illustrate ways students worked. They cannot tell us which assignment builds stronger writing skills.

doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105448.detail: One part of the study asked several AI systems to identify the learning activity described in a study tip. The researchers compared their labels with judgments from human experts.
doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105448.lead: Researchers checked AI-generated study tips for a school reading and writing task. They compared automated checks with expert judgments and found that changing the order of two tips could change which one an AI judge preferred.
doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105448.limit: Agreement with experts on the test material does not show whether a tip helps a pupil learn.

doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103653.detail: The authors organize design choices into six areas, including how apps use personal data, select a response and tailor it to a particular user.
doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103653.lead: A review of AI wellbeing apps asks what information a tool collects about you and how it decides when to step in. The authors use those questions to help designers weigh privacy and personal advice.
doi:10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103653.limit: Some user groups may be underrepresented in the studies reviewed. The framework needs testing with people those studies reached less often.

doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.detail: Across six tasks the team collected responses from 636 people and 37 AI models. In a separate live exchange, judges correctly distinguished one chatbot from a person every time.
doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.lead: Judges correctly identified 67% of human-written photo captions as human and 46% of AI captions as AI. How well they told the two apart depended on the task.
doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.limit: The live result came from a side-by-side comparison with GPT-3.5 Turbo. It cannot tell us whether a reader can recognize an AI-written message seen on its own.

doi:10.1038/s41598-025-01676-x.detail: Respondents at five universities judged their progress on goals such as inclusive teaching and using technology in lessons. Their grade-point averages served a separate purpose in the analysis.
doi:10.1038/s41598-025-01676-x.lead: Among 465 trainee teachers in Wuhan, those who reported using AI more also rated their progress toward teaching goals more highly. The survey asked trainees to judge that progress themselves.
doi:10.1038/s41598-025-01676-x.limit: The researchers neither observed a lesson nor gave an independent teaching test. The survey cannot establish that AI improved classroom performance.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70835-5.detail: Alongside questions about usefulness and trust, students rated how attentive, involved and absorbed they felt while learning.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70835-5.lead: After four weeks of exposure to AI-generated music, university students rated its usefulness and their trust in AI. Those who found the music more useful also reported greater trust.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70835-5.limit: Those judgments came from a survey at one point in time. They cannot establish that playing the music improved attention.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4.detail: Two raters scored students’ exercises without knowing which class produced them or when. Both classes improved in how many ideas students generated and how varied those ideas were.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4.lead: Over twelve weeks, one animation class taught with AI tools made larger gains in the originality and detail of its ideas than a comparison class. The researchers scored a general thinking exercise rather than the animations students made.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4.limit: The comparison used two existing classes. Differences between those classes may also have contributed to the results.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5.detail: Students rated the mental, emotional and physical sides of using digital technology. Their average overall rating was above the midpoint of the seven-point scale.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5.lead: At a university in Ghana, researchers surveyed 212 adult learners and interviewed six about how AI fit into their lives. Nearly all survey respondents had access to a smartphone, and fewer had access to a laptop.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5.limit: The ratings and interviews came from one university. They describe these learners’ experiences and cannot show how AI changed their well-being.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-78895-3.lead: Researchers followed 461 trainee teachers in China. Those who relied more heavily on AI tended to score lower on a measure of their willingness to think critically.

doi:10.1080/00131857.2026.2733624.detail: Kirkham suggests asking students to give reasons for an unfamiliar position, even when an instructor disagrees with the conclusion.
doi:10.1080/00131857.2026.2733624.lead: Drawing on experience teaching philosophy and ethics, the author argues for letting students question uncomfortable ideas and reason together. The essay also asks what happens when educators describe every challenge as a crisis.
doi:10.1080/00131857.2026.2733624.limit: This is a teaching argument grounded in experience. It offers no comparison of classes taught in different ways.

doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261.lead: The authors asked a chatbot a take-home exam question about whether machines think. In their example, getting beyond a polished list of ideas required someone to keep asking for explanations and guidance.

doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2764204.detail: One option in the paper is to ask a student to defend two choices aloud after handing in a 2,000-word case analysis. A teacher could then ask why a specific objection changed the answer.
doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2764204.lead: Kearney imagines grading four versions of the same assignment. Even a complete chat history might show a student accepting every suggestion without revealing whether they could explain the final answer.
doi:10.1080/02602938.2026.2764204.limit: The examples leave open how accurately teachers could judge understanding and how much extra marking time the conversation would take.

doi:10.1080/09297049.2026.2744732.detail: The researchers compared a task designed to feel less stimulating with a more familiar attention task in 28 children and 49 adolescents. The younger children’s false-alarm pattern appeared only on the new task.
doi:10.1080/09297049.2026.2744732.lead: Children and teenagers pressed a button in attention tasks. The timing of their responses varied more with higher ADHD symptom levels, and younger children with more symptoms also made more false alarms in one task.
doi:10.1080/09297049.2026.2744732.limit: The same pattern did not appear among adolescents or on the comparison task. The findings depend on both the age group and the task.

doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522.detail: The reviewers looked separately at how each paper defined critical thinking, how it assessed it and what the authors claimed AI changed.
doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522.lead: A team reviewed 80 papers about how people think critically when using AI. They found that researchers often used the term without defining it, making it hard to tell whether studies measured the same skill.
doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522.limit: The search centered on terms used in human–computer interaction research. Studies using other names for similar skills could have been missed.

doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2732233.detail: Researchers followed 120 English majors for 16 weeks, using writing tests at several points and interviews about how students used the feedback.
doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2732233.lead: At a Chinese university, English majors received writing feedback from AI or a teacher. Over the study, students in the AI group showed greater writing gains, especially in grammar.
doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2732233.limit: The available account comes from the abstract. It does not give enough detail to tell how comparable the groups were before instruction.

doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2744894.detail: The 47 students were enrolled in existing classes. In written accounts, students described ChatGPT as a help with their thinking and a risk to it, sometimes expressing both views at once.
doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2744894.lead: Two groups took the same liberal arts course with the same teacher in different years. Students in the class that used ChatGPT rated their problem solving higher, and described setting limits on when to use it.
doi:10.1080/10494820.2026.2744894.limit: Students took the course in different years and rated their own problem solving. Other differences between the two classes could account for the scores.

doi:10.1093/arclin/acag065.178.detail: The children and teenagers were aged 8 to 17 and had been seen in an outpatient clinic. Differences in how quickly and consistently they responded accounted for much of the link between the tests.
doi:10.1093/arclin/acag065.178.lead: In a clinic sample of 213 children and teenagers, performance on an attention test was linked to errors on another task that required stopping an automatic response or switching rules.
doi:10.1093/arclin/acag065.178.limit: Scores on one test explained only part of the variation in mistakes on the other. These clinic results do not establish how children would respond in a classroom.

doi:10.1111/bjet.70094.detail: In one 25-minute session, 144 Danish high-school students used standard ChatGPT or one of two chatbots that encouraged them to plan and check their work. The version with emotional support also responded to how students felt.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70094.lead: During a 25-minute classroom trial, students using two chatbots designed to guide their work reported more enjoyment and less boredom than students using standard ChatGPT. The groups showed no clear difference in immediate learning gains.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70094.limit: Only 85 students returned for follow-up. Some test scores were inconsistent, which makes the estimate of lasting learning less certain.

doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.detail: At one English college, students had 20 minutes for each set of unfamiliar math problems. They could work with a human tutor, an AI tutor or internet search.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.lead: On the first set of math problems, students with a human tutor started more questions than students with an AI tutor. The study counted attempts and left answer accuracy unmeasured.
doi:10.1111/bjet.70100.limit: One human tutor took part. The researchers counted which questions students started and asked how hard the work felt.

doi:10.1177/21582440261497404.detail: Students also rated how useful AI seemed, how confident they felt using it and how much thinking they handed over. In the researchers’ analysis, these habits had different links with students’ ratings of their own judgment.
doi:10.1177/21582440261497404.lead: In a survey of 976 college students in China, those who trusted AI more also rated their own critical thinking higher. The scores came from students describing how they evaluate information.
doi:10.1177/21582440261497404.limit: Each student completed the questionnaires once. There was no separate test of how well they could evaluate information.

doi:10.1186/s12888-026-08635-4.detail: Researchers compared 24 adults with insomnia and 24 other adults. They asked about everyday flexibility, measured responses to changing rules and scanned brain activity while people viewed general and sleep-related images.
doi:10.1186/s12888-026-08635-4.lead: Adults with insomnia said it was harder to switch their thinking and responded faster overall in a lab task. When the rule changed, the groups showed no clear difference in how much they slowed down or lost accuracy.
doi:10.1186/s12888-026-08635-4.limit: Everyone saw blocks of tasks in a fixed order, which may have affected performance. Differences between the groups do not establish what caused them.

doi:10.1186/s40561-026-00477-7.detail: The review pooled studies covering 16,357 people. The estimated links through motivation and through dependence were close in size, so an overall figure can hide two different patterns.
doi:10.1186/s40561-026-00477-7.lead: A review of 31 studies linked AI use with both a stronger desire to learn and greater dependence on the tool. The two patterns pointed in opposite directions for critical thinking.
doi:10.1186/s40561-026-00477-7.limit: Most studies measured people once. Students already keen to learn may reach for AI more often, and the results cannot tell us which came first.

doi:10.1186/s41239-024-00447-4.lead: Researchers built a version of ChatGPT that gives students hints and asks them to try an answer. It also keeps a log so students can revisit the questions they asked.

doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00632-7.lead: In a television production course, two groups of students followed a sequence of questions when they used AI. Both groups earned higher course grades than students who chose questions freely.

doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00644-3.detail: Eighty-five studies could identify something a student handed over to AI. A more revealing example followed a student who looked at an AI edit and decided to restore their own terminology.
doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00644-3.lead: Of 93 studies in a review, only four documented both how students responded to AI suggestions and how they performed without AI. That leaves a gap between seeing who used the tool and knowing what they learned.
doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00644-3.limit: Of 44 studies describing a student’s response to AI, half relied on recollections or the researchers’ account. Longer-term changes in what students could do alone remain uncertain.

doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1282.lead: After Amazon introduced AI summaries of customer reviews, shoppers contributed more reviews. They wrote about features the summaries missed and added detail about ones already mentioned.

doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1431.detail: In the apartment task, agents decided whether to delegate a case before seeing the AI’s estimate. When they saw explanations of how it worked, the share they delegated rose from 41% to 54%.
doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1431.lead: Real estate agents who saw how an AI priced apartments were less overconfident and handed more cases to it. Researchers saw no clear improvement in how accurately the agents priced apartments on their own.
doi:10.1287/isre.2024.1431.limit: The agents received no feedback between decisions. They might make different choices after seeing which estimates were accurate.

doi:10.14742/ajet.11584.detail: The dashboard used information about students’ online activity to offer feedback. Researchers counted logins alongside course outcomes, and students also described how useful and personal the feedback felt.
doi:10.14742/ajet.11584.lead: In a 12-week study of 180 undergraduates, researchers compared teacher feedback with AI feedback designed to help students reflect. They reported gains in measures including time on task and school performance with the AI approach.
doi:10.14742/ajet.11584.limit: The available abstract gives no information about whether the gains lasted after the 12-week course. A login count alone cannot tell us what a student understood.

doi:10.1515/humaff-2026-0011.detail: The authors describe six possible steps through which trust in a tool could lead someone to hand over more of a task. They ask which parts of the work people would still know how to do if the tool disappeared.
doi:10.1515/humaff-2026-0011.lead: The author proposes six steps by which getting useful help from AI might lead someone to hand over more of their thinking. The paper leaves open whether people actually follow that path over time.
doi:10.1515/humaff-2026-0011.limit: The paper presents a proposed sequence. It did not follow people through those six steps or measure any loss of skill.

doi:10.26300/80wn-ca81.detail: The updated review added 32 papers to its March collection. Across the studies, students sometimes rated AI more favorably than their learning scores would suggest.
doi:10.26300/80wn-ca81.lead: A Stanford team reviewed 52 studies of AI in education. Some found that students learned less when AI completed their work, while guided practice and tutoring showed more promise across studies, with mixed results.
doi:10.26300/80wn-ca81.limit: Only five newly added studies of student-facing tools took place in US elementary or secondary schools. Teachers in those settings have fewer direct comparisons to draw on.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2025.1697554.detail: In the proposed design, the AI can respond as a confused learner. That gives the student a reason to supply a missing step in an explanation.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2025.1697554.lead: The authors propose a tutor that plays the learner. A student explains an idea to the AI, and the AI can ask a follow-up question that invites the student to rethink the explanation.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2025.1697554.limit: A classroom test would be needed to tell whether explaining an idea to the AI helps a student use it later.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1861548.detail: One group described both checking AI carefully and relying on it. Those two habits could occur in the same learner.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1861548.lead: A survey of 848 learners found several ways of working with AI. Some described evaluating its answers closely, while others relied on them with little checking or remained skeptical and used AI very little.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1861548.limit: The questionnaire asked about habits at a single point. The answers cannot establish whether checking a tool changes how much people rely on it.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1878665.detail: The reviewers compared studies that described AI giving plausible but false answers with accounts of students consulting another source to check a claim.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1878665.lead: Across 26 studies of college students using AI, researchers found accounts of students checking sources after encountering convincing errors or invented citations. The review could not tell how often students checked.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1878665.limit: The studies used different methods, so they do not give a common estimate of how much a particular checking exercise helps.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1894455.lead: Future computing teachers at a university in Kazakhstan used ChatGPT on programming assignments. Although they said checking AI-generated code was important, their written accounts often gave few details about how they checked it.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1918374.detail: The authors organized studies published from 2018 to 2026 around decisions such as who plans the work and who checks whether it succeeded.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1918374.lead: A review of higher education research found that AI sometimes helped students spot gaps and sometimes took over decisions about how to study. Much of the research came from settings with ample resources.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1918374.limit: The review describes patterns across studies. It cannot give a size for the learning gain from using a particular tool.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1929091.detail: The questionnaire also asked about learning anxiety and other people’s influence. The researchers found a small link involving anxiety and no clear link between social influence and plans to use AI.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1929091.lead: Among 350 university students in Ghana, those who expected AI to be useful and easy to use were more likely to say they intended to use it. The survey asked about plans.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1929091.limit: Everyone answered once. The survey cannot show whether reducing anxiety would change what tools students go on to use.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1944529.detail: Imagine a challenging writing task. In the authors’ framework, the experience depends in part on whether a teacher helps students work through it or simply sets the bar high.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1944529.lead: The authors propose a way for writing teachers to combine demanding assignments with support for students using AI. They describe four combinations of expectations and support.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1944529.limit: These four classroom settings are proposals drawn from earlier writing and learning research. They still need testing with teachers and writers.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1949276.lead: Twenty students across four Latin American countries chose pictures to explain how they use AI at university. Some described it as a quiet companion and others described relief at getting help alongside unease about academic honesty.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1952725.detail: The survey followed a semester of classroom activity and asked about familiarity with AI, benefits students thought it offered, and awareness of ethical issues.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1952725.lead: Undergraduates used AI to prepare short lessons and teach their classmates. In questionnaires afterward, students said AI made learning easier and more enjoyable.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1952725.limit: The survey records students’ views after the activity. It cannot show whether teaching the lessons improved their reasoning.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1953305.detail: The author analyzed four publications from UNESCO and the OECD, asking how their words assign responsibility to students, teachers and institutions.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1953305.lead: The author examines how international policy documents define cheating with AI and who they hold responsible when someone uses it in academic work.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1953305.limit: The evidence is the wording of public documents. It leaves open how individual universities enforce rules or how students respond.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1971754.detail: A student starts by identifying what a passage needs to say, considers different ways of expressing it and looks back on the wording they kept. Teachers can use those explanations when discussing a revision.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1971754.lead: The authors propose a writing exercise in which students draw on more than one language, compare their wording with AI suggestions and explain what they choose.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1971754.limit: The authors offer the exercise as a teaching proposal. They do not report whether trying it improved students’ writing or judgment.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1981900.detail: Salameh brought together experiments, surveys and essays. One question running through the review is whether a polished answer lets a teacher tell who judged the evidence behind it.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1981900.lead: Walid Salameh reviewed 45 sources to ask what universities should teach when students can quickly find or generate an answer. The sources used different ways to assess thinking.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1981900.limit: One reviewer chose and coded the sources. The review may have missed relevant studies, and it gives no single estimate of how AI affects thinking.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1983044.lead: Ten first-year students described creating AI images for a course assignment. They said choosing and judging the images helped them connect ideas from class. The study asked about their experience.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1997466.detail: The editors bring together four papers. One review found more consistent benefits for making a plan than for carrying it out. Another paper compared AI feedback with feedback from classmates in Hong Kong.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1997466.lead: The authors of this editorial ask how students could use AI to plan their work and interpret feedback while still deciding what to do next.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1997466.limit: The editorial uses these papers to pose questions for teaching. It contributes no new classroom test of its own.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955.detail: The 60 students took English tests and separately answered questions about motivation and how they managed their studies. The tests and questionnaires measured different parts of the experience.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955.lead: Two university English classes in China took tests ten weeks apart. Scores rose in both classes, and the class using Duolingo gained more than the class using textbooks and teacher-led exercises.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955.limit: The classes used different teaching approaches for ten weeks. The comparison leaves open which particular feature helped and whether the gains lasted.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1598867.detail: Both groups took singing lessons and submitted recordings. Researchers analyzed data from 80 of the 100 trainees originally assigned to groups.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1598867.lead: Trainee teachers who compared recordings, used a chatbot and kept a journal reported larger gains in managing their singing practice. Both groups sang better after six weeks, with no clear difference in how much they improved.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1598867.limit: The additional activities came as a package. The study cannot identify what the chatbot contributed on its own.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1666974.detail: The team tried a draft questionnaire with 241 people and checked the resulting structure with another 305. Students who reported more strain also reported more writing anxiety.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1666974.lead: What makes writing in a second language with AI feel demanding? Researchers developed an 18-question survey covering tasks such as giving instructions, checking suggestions and fitting them into a draft.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1666974.limit: The questionnaire asks writers how demanding the work feels. Its scores do not tell a teacher how well a particular passage was written.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1699320.detail: The authors contrast a reminder that takes something off a person’s mind with feedback that invites the person to keep checking how they feel.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1699320.lead: A chatbot can offer advice about stress, but keeping track of its advice can itself take effort. Ginto Chirayath and colleagues ask when that extra work helps people cope and when it becomes a burden.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1699320.limit: The examples illustrate possible uses. They do not tell us how often a tool eases or adds to someone’s strain.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1822091.lead: Among 878 university students in China, those who used AI more often also described depending on it more. Students who reported greater dependence gave themselves lower ratings for critical thinking.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832219.detail: The authors bring together research on smartphone habits and on restrictions in schools. One concerns how individual teenagers use phones, while the other concerns what happens under a school policy.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832219.lead: A review of research on teenagers’ phones found links between heavy use and modest attention and sleep difficulties. Studies of what happened when schools banned phones gave mixed results.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832219.limit: The studies differ in setting and design. The review cannot isolate how much a ban itself changes teenagers’ sleep or attention.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1870626.lead: Researchers surveyed Chinese university students three times over eight weeks. Students who reported greater reliance on AI at the start tended to report less confidence in their ability to learn four weeks later.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1873941.detail: Researchers randomly assigned 45 people to work with sounds and images and 42 to work without them. Participants also rated how demanding the tasks felt.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1873941.lead: In a lab study, 87 adults did short tasks with or without intermittent sounds and images. Researchers found no clear overall increase in errors when participants had to remember information or hold back an automatic response.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1873941.limit: These tasks lasted a short time. The findings leave open what happens during a longer period of interrupted work.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1878629.detail: Researchers surveyed 589 students and people early in their careers on three occasions. Both ways of using AI were linked to similar immediate benefits in their accounts.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1878629.lead: People who said they handed the thinking over to AI also reported less interest in the work itself. Those who described using AI as a helper while making their own decisions reported more interest.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1878629.limit: These were people’s views of their abilities. The survey did not test what they could do independently.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1884676.detail: The team began with 26 possible questions and used answers from 665 students to decide which ones belonged together. They then tested that structure with a separate group.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1884676.lead: Researchers tested a questionnaire that asks Chinese college students which parts of learning they hand to AI. A second group of 1,123 students helped check how the questions worked together.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1884676.limit: The scores describe which tasks students say they delegate. This study cannot tell whether delegating a task changes a student’s skill over time.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199.detail: The study followed 168 students and scored a final supervised writing task. That gave the researchers a way to compare assisted drafts with later work in the same genre.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199.lead: Across six writing classes, students with open access to AI produced the strongest assisted drafts. Students who had limits on AI help and reflected on their decisions later wrote the strongest essays on their own.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199.limit: Whole classes received different kinds of support. The group with limits on AI also had to reflect, so the two features cannot be separated.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1913577.detail: The researchers analyzed 797 completed questionnaires. Students rated their habits of questioning information as well as how much thinking they felt AI helped them do or took over.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1913577.lead: Students at six Chinese universities rated the gap between what they could finish with AI and what they thought they could do alone. These were students’ own judgments.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1913577.limit: The study never compared the same student’s performance on matched tasks with and without AI. It cannot establish the size of an actual skills gap.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1915597.detail: The authors distinguish feeling calmer during a conversation from being able to manage a different situation later. They suggest following the person over time to see whether a skill carries over.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1915597.lead: The authors suggest a test for chatbot support in later life. If someone practices a way to cope with a difficult situation during a chat, can they use it on their own later?
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1915597.limit: The article proposes a way to evaluate chatbots. It reports no trial with older adults.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920791.detail: The students came from one university in Shenzhen. The lesson required them to picture how three-dimensional pieces fit together, and they also rated how much mental effort it took.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920791.lead: Forty students watched a short video about how wooden joints fit together. Adding motion to the AI-generated images made no clear difference to scores on a ten-question test.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920791.limit: The effort rating reflects what watching the lesson felt like. It cannot identify which part of the video made the task demanding.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920947.detail: The analysis grouped examples from doctoral research into five stages of working with AI. Tasks included using it to explain a concept, suggest methods and revise writing.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920947.lead: The researchers studied how doctoral students in China checked AI-assisted work that they would have to defend themselves. They traced the steps between asking for help with a research task and taking responsibility for the finished argument.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920947.limit: The accounts came from doctoral students at Chinese research universities. They leave open how students in other programs handle the same tasks.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924393.detail: The three-month study matched students on factors such as prior grades. A 40-question test covered skills including judging arguments, spotting assumptions and drawing conclusions.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924393.lead: In one data science course, students who received structured AI feedback scored higher on a later thinking test than similar students who received instructor feedback. The classes also differed in how feedback was given.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1924393.limit: One class received four stages of feedback with AI and the other received usual instructor feedback. Matching students cannot separate the source of feedback from its structure.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929666.detail: The survey compared the kinds of prompts workers preferred with their confidence in working with AI and the mental effort they reported. It also asked whether professional experience changed those relationships.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929666.lead: Researchers asked 1,760 people who work with specialized terms how they give instructions to AI and how demanding that work feels.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929666.limit: The responses describe preferences and perceived effort. They cannot tell which prompting approach produces the most accurate term in practice.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.detail: The researchers combined two surveys covering 799 adolescents. Their analysis examined which reported habits and experiences were most useful for predicting school difficulties in those data.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.lead: Across two surveys of 799 teenagers, stress and time spent on social media stood out in predicting reported school difficulties. The surveys cannot tell whether either factor caused those difficulties.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.limit: Both surveys relied on accounts given at one point in time. They cannot establish whether stress or time on social media led to later school difficulties.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286.detail: At universities in mainland China, 421 undergraduates filled in paper questionnaires about AI use and feedback during the 2024–2025 academic year.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286.lead: University students rated how they used AI feedback, reflected on their work and judged information. The link between handling feedback and reported critical thinking varied with how much students said they reflected.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286.limit: All responses came from one point in time. The order in which students developed these habits remains unclear.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1941348.lead: Foreign-language students who feared falling behind or felt emotionally attached to AI were more likely to say they depended on it too much. The study surveyed 249 students at one Chinese vocational college.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1948254.detail: Six classes worked on a four-week design project. Researchers examined AI conversations and had judges score work by 54 teams, alongside students’ own reports of confidence and involvement.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1948254.lead: In one classroom project, students given steps for using AI asked it to compare and critique ideas more often. They asked it to finish answers for them less often.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1948254.limit: Whole classes followed each approach. Differences between the classes and the short project make it hard to tell whether the same students would work differently on another task.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955418.detail: The 529 respondents already had experience using AI for coursework. Those who felt more able to adapt to academic demands also reported taking a more active part in learning.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955418.lead: In a survey at a Chinese university, students who felt more stressed by AI also reported more difficulty adjusting to academic demands and less involvement in learning. The survey could not tell which came first.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955418.limit: The students came from one university. The link between stress and participation may look different elsewhere.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1962253.detail: After eight weeks, the chatbot class reported larger drops in physical signs of anxiety and in avoiding writing. Researchers found no clear group differences for worries about tests, time pressure or self-doubt.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1962253.lead: Some students who used a chatbot in an English writing class said it made asking for help less stressful. The study measured worry about writing and did not score the writing itself.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1962253.limit: Only two classes took part, and chatbot use was part of a broader set of lessons. The comparison cannot isolate the chatbot’s contribution.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1971672.detail: Students who reported more mental strain also tended to rate their AI knowledge and problem-solving skills lower. The researchers compared these ratings across vocational colleges in Guangdong.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1971672.lead: Researchers at six Chinese vocational colleges compared students’ ratings of their AI skills, mental workload and ability to solve difficult problems. Students rated their own problem-solving skills.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1971672.limit: The ratings cannot show how well students would solve an unfamiliar problem in class or on the job.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.detail: The authors brought together 51 studies. They describe a cycle in which learners monitor their work, decide how much to trust AI feedback and then choose how much of the next step to hand over.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.lead: A review of AI in language learning looks at what students do after a tool gives feedback. The authors trace how trust enters decisions to accept a suggestion, check it, change it or reject it.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.limit: The review searched two databases. Studies listed only in specialist education or psychology databases may be missing.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975833.detail: In one experiment, the team compared people receiving more or less AI help. A nine-question scale asked about the planning and checking they did on that particular task.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975833.lead: Across four experiments, researchers studied how much people planned, checked their progress and reflected while working with AI. The experiments followed those habits during the task.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975833.limit: A brief reduction in checking during an experiment does not tell us whether someone loses that habit or becomes less creative over time.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1978175.detail: The participants were e-commerce students studying how to develop computer systems. Students who felt more confident in their abilities also said they were more involved in their coursework.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1978175.lead: Students in computing courses who rated their AI tools as more capable also described less unnecessary mental effort and greater confidence in their own abilities. The survey captured these views at one point in time.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1978175.limit: The students judged the AI tools’ abilities themselves. The researchers did not use those ratings to test how well the tools actually performed.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1981428.detail: The 1,206 students took an online knowledge test and rated their own AI skills. Their ratings and their scores overlapped only modestly, so confidence gave an incomplete picture of how much they knew.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1981428.lead: Engineering students judged two pieces of flawed AI advice. Those who did better on an AI knowledge test said they checked answers more often, and those reporting more checks gave better engineering answers.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1981428.limit: Students reported their own checking habits, and no one supervised the online assessment. The study cannot establish which came first, checking more often or doing better on the tasks.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989652.detail: The proposed model follows choices a teacher could face, such as checking an AI suggestion, overruling it or seeking another person’s judgment. It asks who is responsible at each step.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989652.lead: The authors propose that clear rules and clear responsibilities can shape how teachers decide when to use AI. They lay out questions researchers could test.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989652.limit: The paper develops predictions from earlier research. It does not follow teachers making these decisions or compare different school rules.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1993658.detail: The team combined 1,461 teenagers’ questionnaires with physical fitness tests and marks in Chinese, math and English. Attention came from the students’ answers, while school marks came from exams.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1993658.lead: Chinese teenagers who said they depended more on AI also reported more trouble directing their attention and earned lower exam scores. The researchers could not tell which came first.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1993658.limit: Students who already struggled to concentrate or with schoolwork may have turned to AI more often.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1997631.detail: The questionnaire asked whether students trusted AI as a tool and whether it fit what they valued in art. Trust had the strongest direct link with plans to use AI among the factors in the model.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1997631.lead: Among 450 Chinese art students, those who trusted AI more were more likely to say they planned to use it. The survey measured intentions.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1997631.limit: The survey cannot show whether trusting the tool led someone to use it or changed the creative decisions they made on an artwork.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1998976.detail: The researchers also asked how closely students kept track of their own understanding. The link between a heavy workload and handing tasks to AI appeared in both the higher- and lower-monitoring groups.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1998976.lead: In a survey of 600 undergraduates, students who said learning took more mental effort also reported handing more of the thinking to AI. The survey cannot establish which came first.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1998976.limit: The answers describe students’ perceptions. The study did not observe the moment a student accepted AI feedback or decided to check it.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1999813.detail: Teachers at universities across six parts of China described how they felt about digital tools and how often they tried new ways of working. Both were linked to being more open to AI.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1999813.lead: In a survey of 807 university physical education teachers, those more open to using AI also reported feeling better at work. The survey captured both at one point in time.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1999813.limit: Teachers volunteered or were referred by others. Their reports cannot show how adopting AI would change other teachers’ working lives.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2003031.lead: University students who read smoother AI explanations expected to do better on a test. In that experiment, researchers found no clear difference between groups when students took the test on their own.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2006519.detail: Researchers surveyed 486 university students learning English and interviewed 20. The interviews explored who decided which feedback to keep and how students judged its usefulness.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2006519.lead: Some university writers described using AI for a quick polish. Others described weighing its suggestions before deciding what to change in their English writing.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2006519.limit: The study relies on what students remembered and reported. It cannot show whether their writing improved because of the way they used feedback.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2007654.detail: Across two classes, 126 students discussed problems in their existing groups and then answered four questions on their own. The researchers also asked how well students thought they had done and found no clear group difference in that judgment.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2007654.lead: Students whose groups could use AI during a discussion scored slightly higher on a short individual test immediately afterward. The researchers did not give a later test to see what students remembered.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2007654.limit: Students had little room to improve near the top of the short test. The researchers also lacked a test of students’ starting level.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011342.detail: Students at three institutions in Guangdong answered questions about relying on AI, keeping up their effort, and how much they felt they had learned. Greater reliance had only a small link with lower ratings of learning.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011342.lead: Among 982 university students in China, those who described themselves as more dependent on AI also reported more trouble keeping up their study effort. Students rated their own learning.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011342.limit: The study collected these answers at the same time. It cannot tell whether struggling to keep up led students to depend more on AI or whether reliance came first.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2011597.lead: Among 530 medical students surveyed in China, about a third fell into a group that relied on AI for thinking through tasks yet reported little trouble putting work off. Another group reported both dependence and procrastination.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2013021.detail: The study compared 12,191 students with peers at the same school. Using AI to help learn was linked to higher science scores, while using it to summarize, look up new topics or draft assignments was linked to lower scores.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2013021.lead: Among 15-year-olds in four Chinese regions, science scores differed with the reason students gave for using AI. The study could not tell whether using it changed their scores.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2013021.limit: Students chose their own reasons for using AI. They could already have differed in confidence, preparation or how much help they needed.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2015390.detail: The researchers selected five cases from a group of 42 trainees. They combined screen recordings with spoken explanations, interviews and written reflections to follow decisions about what to include in a lesson.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2015390.lead: Five trainee math teachers in China used AI to plan lessons. In four decisions across two teachers, they spotted something uncertain and asked the same AI to check its own answer.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2015390.limit: Watching decisions in five selected cases can reveal how a problem arises. It gives no estimate of how common that problem is among trainee teachers.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2017882.detail: The study began with 850 music students and retained 718. Students also rated how well they understood and managed emotions, giving researchers a way to track how those ratings changed alongside class involvement.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2017882.lead: Music students at four Chinese universities answered five surveys about AI-assisted classes. Those who grew more involved in class also tended to say they became more absorbed in what they were doing.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2017882.limit: Several ratings changed together. This leaves open whether becoming more absorbed in class helped students handle emotions or whether something else changed both.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2022639.lead: Researchers examined online discussions about grading in the age of AI, mostly from Reddit. Detecting AI use and supervising work in class featured prominently. The counts describe what people discussed.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024279.detail: The researchers surveyed 475 graduate students three times. The link between feeling swamped and feeling tired was weaker among students who often handed simple tasks, such as summarizing papers, to AI.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024279.lead: Graduate students who felt overwhelmed by AI suggestions for English writing reported more mental fatigue two weeks later. Four weeks later, they expressed less interest in using AI again.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024279.limit: The last survey asked whether students planned to use AI again. The researchers did not track what they chose next.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2024870.lead: Researchers surveyed students at three Chinese universities twice, twelve weeks apart. Those who reported making greater use of AI writing feedback later rated themselves higher at managing their English writing.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2041306.detail: Looking up facts and making outlines were among the tasks students handed over. Those who described putting effort into understanding ideas also reported greater engagement, a different pattern from the burden of checking AI output.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2041306.lead: A survey of 1,050 students asked what work they handed to AI. Students who found checking its answers burdensome also reported feeling less engaged in their studies.
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.2041306.limit: The researchers did not watch students verify answers or test what they could remember.

doi:10.3390/educsci13090856.detail: The researchers kept the interview transcript and examined the challenges the chatbot named, including plagiarism and how educators might respond. They used these answers to discuss possible university policies.
doi:10.3390/educsci13090856.lead: The researchers interviewed ChatGPT about its place in higher education and analyzed its answers about issues such as academic honesty. The interview shows how the chatbot described these concerns.
doi:10.3390/educsci13090856.limit: A chatbot’s account cannot establish how often students cheat or whether a university policy prevents cheating.

doi:10.3390/educsci13100998.detail: ChatGPT suggested how much time to spend on each activity and labeled its example lesson as intermediate. A teacher could review both choices against what a particular class already knows.
doi:10.3390/educsci13100998.lead: Researchers examined a lesson plan produced by ChatGPT. It included a warm-up, practice activities and a final assessment, giving teachers a draft they could adapt for their own classes.
doi:10.3390/educsci13100998.limit: The researchers analyzed a generated plan. They did not observe the lesson being taught or students using its materials.

doi:10.3390/educsci14020120.detail: The researchers tried prompts for several parts of studying, including planning the work, finding materials and checking understanding. They inspected the examples and explanations ChatGPT returned.
doi:10.3390/educsci14020120.lead: Researchers asked ChatGPT to help plan and explain programming lessons. It produced study schedules and examples, giving the authors a way to examine the advice a learner might receive.
doi:10.3390/educsci14020120.limit: The evidence comes from the tool’s replies. The study did not follow students learning to write or debug programs on their own.

doi:10.3390/educsci16081291.detail: Rowe suggests looking at the particular skill a student has demonstrated. Someone ready to delegate one familiar step may still need practice doing another step alone.
doi:10.3390/educsci16081291.lead: Luke Rowe proposes that students first practice a skill on their own, then try it with limited AI help. Once students show what they can do, teachers could let them hand over selected tasks.
doi:10.3390/educsci16081291.limit: The three stages form a teaching proposal. Their effects still need classroom testing.

doi:10.3390/educsci16091470.detail: Interviewees suggested comparing human and AI answers and asking students to explain a decision aloud without AI. These are educators’ ideas for making students’ reasoning visible.
doi:10.3390/educsci16091470.lead: Seventeen medical educators in the Netherlands discussed where AI might help students and when it could take over too much of their thinking. The interviews capture teachers’ concerns about what students can do independently.
doi:10.3390/educsci16091470.limit: The researchers interviewed educators. They did not directly assess students making clinical decisions.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14070116.detail: In a survey of 353 students, 22.4% agreed that they sometimes accepted AI-generated material without checking it critically.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14070116.lead: Some Chinese university students who described using AI in more involved ways also said they relied on it more. The survey asked students to judge their own thinking skills.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14070116.limit: The survey recorded what students remembered doing. Researchers could not observe from those answers which suggestions students actually checked.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080175.detail: The tests included remembering sequences of digits, solving visual patterns and finding a word that linked several other words.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080175.lead: Young adults described how often they used several kinds of media at once, then took thinking tests. Researchers found little overall link, though heavier multitaskers did slightly worse on a word-association task.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080175.limit: Participants estimated their own media use. The study cannot tell whether switching media affected their scores or whether people with different skills used media differently.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080182.detail: The survey asked separately about anxiety around AI, habitual reliance on it and concern about losing control over lesson design. The answers distinguished general anxiety from that specific worry.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080182.lead: Among 239 trainee teachers surveyed in eastern China, those who said they relied more on AI also worried more about whether their lesson designs were truly their own.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14080182.limit: The teachers volunteered and answered once. Their reports cannot establish whether reliance preceded the worry or the worry preceded reliance.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14100254.detail: One teacher compared several AI answers while preparing a lesson, then collected students’ phones so they could work through a problem on their own first. The researchers interviewed 22 teachers and used documents for three others.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14100254.lead: University teachers in China described how they used their subject knowledge to check AI answers and asked students to explain their choices. The interviews tell us how teachers described checking, rather than how often it happened.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14100254.limit: The researchers prompted teachers to discuss checking. Teachers who volunteered through an AI-focused professional community may describe different routines from other teachers.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110286.detail: The same students wrote two timed compositions, one with access to AI and one without. They answered the same prompt both times, allowing the researchers to compare each writer’s wording across conditions.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110286.lead: Thirty-eight students writing in Russian used longer words and more words that linked ideas when they could use AI. The researchers found no clear difference in total word count.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110286.limit: Repeating a prompt could change how someone writes the second time. The finished essays leave open whether students could use the new wording independently later.

doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110288.detail: The researchers grouped respondents by how they assessed their skills and the resources available to them. These groups differed in how prepared the trainees felt to try new teaching approaches.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110288.lead: A survey of 942 trainee teachers asked about skills such as judging the quality of AI answers. Those who rated their skills and resources higher also gave themselves higher marks for trying new ways to teach.
doi:10.3390/jintelligence14110288.limit: The researchers did not observe the trainees teaching a class. A high self-rating leaves open what a trainee would do in front of students.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38910.detail: The researchers analyzed 891 responses, including 645 from the US and 246 from Türkiye. Once the model included how students coordinated and revised their work, it showed no clear direct link between confidence and reported checking.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38910.lead: College students in the US and Türkiye described how they worked with AI and whether they questioned its answers. The survey linked reworking AI-assisted tasks with reporting that they checked the output.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38910.limit: Students volunteered and answered once. Several questions asked about overlapping habits, making it difficult to separate which habits came first.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38950.detail: The team enrolled 112 students and coded 880 exchanges about math. For the comparison with test scores, 89 students had the necessary records. Asking for help was common, but a chat transcript only captured what students put into words.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38950.lead: Ninth graders in three German schools practiced math with a chatbot before solving problems without it. The researchers traced when students asked how to do a problem, but conflicting statistics leave the link with test scores uncertain.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38950.limit: This was one practice session and an immediate test. It leaves open whether the same students would remember the material later.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38990.detail: After about 20 minutes solving quadratic equations, participants discussed what made the chatbot feel like a partner. They disagreed about whether its mistakes made it seem more approachable or simply less useful.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38990.lead: Seven researchers tried an AI math partner while playing the role of students. They said it helped to have room to try their own ideas, and described how getting the answer too soon could spoil that exchange.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.38990.limit: Researchers played the students’ roles. The interviews leave open how actual students would respond or how much math they would learn.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14833v1.detail: On the final challenge, the researchers picked a question each person had already answered correctly. When participants had received feedback on earlier answers, the adviser’s track record made a difference to how persuasive it was.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14833v1.lead: After chatting with an AI adviser, people sometimes changed an answer they had gotten right. Without feedback on earlier answers, a previously inaccurate adviser persuaded them on 48% of the final trials.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14833v1.limit: The experiments followed people through short factual tasks. They leave open whether trust would change for longer or more consequential decisions.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15732v1.detail: The 121 participants considered eight moral dilemmas before choosing advisers for future tasks. That let the researchers distinguish agreement with someone’s reasons from willingness to give them control of the decision.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15732v1.lead: People choosing an adviser for imagined decisions were more willing to hear AI advice than to let AI act for them. They declined AI in 12% of choices about getting advice and 38% of choices about handing over the decision.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15732v1.limit: Participants described choices they would make in imagined situations. The study did not follow anyone handing over an actual decision.

url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16667v1.detail: The experiment included 572 people, some acting as human advisers. Decision makers could discuss the split with an adviser or choose on their own, allowing the researchers to compare impressions of the advice with the amount pledged.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16667v1.lead: People deciding how much of a potential £97 prize to donate rated AI advice more trustworthy than human advice. Researchers found no clear difference in the sums pledged by people receiving AI advice, human advice or no advice.
url:https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16667v1.limit: Each person faced one decision tied to a lottery. The results leave room for different responses in other settings.

url:https://developer.apple.com/document.detail: Apple gives the example of separating email accounts during a Work Focus. An app with the right filter can let work alerts through while keeping personal ones quiet.
url:https://developer.apple.com/document.lead: Apple lets developers change what an app shows when a Focus is on. The choices a person sees depend on which filters the app supports.
url:https://developer.apple.com/document.limit: The documentation explains what app developers can support. It does not test whether filtering alerts improves anyone’s concentration.

url:https://feedback.one-sec.app/en/help.detail: The Observatory raises a question for testing: after someone picks a reason, do they still open the app? That decision would tell us more than simply counting completed prompts.
url:https://feedback.one-sec.app/en/help.lead: The one sec app can ask why you want to open another app. You make that choice at the moment you reach for it.
url:https://feedback.one-sec.app/en/help.limit: The source describes a product feature. It leaves open whether repeated prompts change habits or become an extra tap people ignore.

url:https://freedom.to/.detail: The scheduled block lets someone make the decision before a planned work period. One trade-off for the reader to consider is what happens if a blocked communication app is needed mid-session.
url:https://freedom.to/.lead: Freedom lets you choose sites or apps to block for a set time. A session can cover more than one device.
url:https://freedom.to/.limit: The feature description does not measure whether people concentrated better or whether another device or activity took the place of the blocked app.

url:https://openalex.org/W7127755367.detail: The reviewers propose six ideas to test about how campus rules could affect students’ confidence and how much thinking they do themselves.
url:https://openalex.org/W7127755367.lead: A review of 73 studies compares what happens when universities restrict AI, allow it freely, or guide students in using it. The authors offer questions for testing how those policies relate to effort and confidence.
url:https://openalex.org/W7127755367.limit: The accessible abstract describes the policy categories but gives no estimate of what would change if a university switched policies.

url:https://openalex.org/W7161620989.detail: The proposed interviews would examine how a chatbot’s human-like presence relates to trust and which decisions workers hand over to it.
url:https://openalex.org/W7161620989.lead: Would employees check a chatbot’s answer less carefully if talking to it felt like talking to a colleague? The authors propose interviewing employees and managers to explore that question.
url:https://openalex.org/W7161620989.limit: The abstract describes planned interviews. It contains no observations of employees changing their decisions.

url:https://openalex.org/W7164777577.detail: The researchers also included readers who faced distractions without a blocker and readers who faced no distractions. These groups give a reference for interpreting eye movements during the task.
url:https://openalex.org/W7164777577.lead: Researchers tracked readers’ eye movements while they read under different conditions. Some readers could block digital distractions themselves, while others had the distractions blocked for them.
url:https://openalex.org/W7164777577.limit: The accessible abstract ends before the results are described. It cannot support a conclusion about which blocking method worked better.

url:https://www.amny.com/politics/google.detail: Google’s education chief said that turning off AI entirely would also remove access to Search on school-managed accounts. The council wanted to know how administrators could carry out the city’s policy for younger students.
url:https://www.amny.com/politics/google.lead: New York City schools disabled two Google AI tools on student Chromebooks, yet students reportedly still saw AI summaries in Search. City Council members asked Google if schools could turn those off and keep Search.
url:https://www.amny.com/politics/google.limit: The council asked for a written answer by November 19. When the article appeared, Google had yet to reply to the newspaper.

url:https://www.android.com/productivity.detail: Android’s guide describes using the activity view to choose a daily limit, or scheduling a period when particular apps should pause. Someone concerned about interruptions can start by looking at which app sends the most alerts.
url:https://www.android.com/productivity.lead: Android’s Focus Mode lets you pause selected apps. Its activity records show time spent on the phone and how many alerts arrived.
url:https://www.android.com/productivity.limit: Time spent in an app tells you how long it was open. It does not tell you whether you were concentrating on the task you meant to do.

url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.detail: The guide suggests giving beginners a first try at a task before they compare their work with an AI answer. It also asks managers to notice when checking spills into time outside work.
url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.lead: The American Psychological Association asks employers to give people time to check AI-assisted decisions and opportunities to practice the skills that checking requires.
url:https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-.limit: These are suggestions for workplace design. The guide does not test how much time a particular team will need.

url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.detail: One Denver professor moved writing into class so he could watch an argument take shape. That left less class time for teaching political science.
url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.lead: One Colorado student asked AI to help revise an essay using a teacher’s feedback. Another used it to check mechanics while keeping the voice of a college essay.
url:https://www.cpr.org/2026/11/18/stude.limit: The reporting describes choices teachers and students made. It does not measure what students learned.

url:https://www.edsurge.com/news/ai-has-.detail: Shuller considered having students compare vocabulary maps with AI-generated versions. That lesson stayed on paper, while shared annotation gave the class time to discuss the meaning of a particular passage.
url:https://www.edsurge.com/news/ai-has-.lead: Seventh-grade teacher Court Shuller describes having students draft on paper and discuss ideas aloud. The account explains the classroom choice and what the teacher observed.
url:https://www.edsurge.com/news/ai-has-.limit: The teacher changed laptop use more broadly. The account cannot separate the effects of removing AI from the effects of removing other screen distractions.

url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/ha.detail: The Harvard team drew on more than 5,000 pieces of research on child development. The educators Langreo interviewed wanted practical guidance and raised questions about how to apply it in class.
