url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/ha.lead: Lauraine Langreo reports on guidance for matching AI use to a child’s age and the skill they are practicing. Getting another practice problem gives a child a different job from receiving the homework answer.
url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/ha.limit: The number of sources describes the background research. It does not count trials of AI tools with children.

url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/is.detail: Interviewees discussed chances to use AI for student practice and teacher feedback. They emphasized that a school choosing a tool needs to know the assignment, who will use it, and what skill the lesson is meant to develop.
url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/is.lead: Sarah Schwartz asks researchers what schools can learn from studies of AI in classrooms. Getting a chatbot to explain a problem leaves a student with a different task from getting it to complete the assignment.
url:https://www.edweek.org/technology/is.limit: Schwartz reports on the Stanford review. Counting the news article alongside that review as a second test would count the same evidence twice.

url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.detail: EFF describes how someone appealing a removal could supply context that the automated system missed. It also points to languages with less training material as a case where moderation tools may work unevenly.
url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.lead: The Electronic Frontier Foundation argues that people whose posts are removed by an automated system should be able to appeal to a person. An appeal gives them a chance to explain context the system missed.
url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.limit: The essay proposes ways to oversee moderation. It does not measure how often people win appeals or which safeguards reduce mistaken removals.

url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.detail: EFF reports that keeping Messages out of Siri removes its message-reading and reply features. The example shows readers what they might give up when they limit assistant access to a particular app.
url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.lead: The Electronic Frontier Foundation explains what it says happens when people exclude messaging apps from Siri AI. For example, keeping Messages out also means giving up Siri’s ability to read and reply to messages.
url:https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/1.limit: The account describes settings as EFF reported them. It does not independently test the software or establish which options are available on every device.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/how-ai-.detail: The essay discusses attention-monitoring headbands in schools and trials of emotion detection at borders. It asks who has the power to question a system’s label.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/how-ai-.lead: The author asks what happens when a school treats a system’s guess about a student’s attention or emotions as a basis for decisions. The article examines who gets to interpret those signals.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/how-ai-.limit: The examples support an argument about oversight. They do not establish how accurately a particular device measures attention.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/new-per.detail: The authors distinguish an assistant’s skill at carrying out a task from its loyalty to the person it represents. A capable tool could still act in a platform’s interest.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/new-per.lead: Richard Reisman and Richard Whitt propose giving people an AI assistant that helps decide what appears in their feeds. They ask how recommendations would change if users controlled whom the assistant serves.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/new-per.limit: Their proposed “attention guardians” have yet to demonstrate an improvement in focus or wellbeing in this account.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/the-int.detail: The authors discuss ways a service could check that an assistant has permission for a particular action before carrying it out.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/the-int.lead: When an AI tool acts for someone online, who gets to decide what it can do? This policy essay asks how people can direct those actions and who should answer for them.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/the-int.limit: This policy essay proposes ways to assign responsibility. It does not test whether a permission system prevents unwanted actions.

url:https://www.techpolicy.press/when-an.detail: Rida imagines a digital wallet that lets an assistant spend up to €100. A merchant could inspect that permission before accepting a purchase, and a buyer could refer to it in a dispute.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/when-an.lead: When an AI shopping assistant clicks to buy, how does the seller know what the buyer agreed to? Camillia Rida argues that sellers need to know which decisions the buyer authorized.
url:https://www.techpolicy.press/when-an.limit: The spending limit is an example. The essay does not test whether wallets prevent unwanted purchases.

url:https://www.theguardian.com/commenti.detail: Kirman recognizes the appeal of a patient tutor for a teenager who has little access to one. She asks whether even a tutor that answers with questions can crowd out time a student would otherwise spend working alone.
url:https://www.theguardian.com/commenti.lead: Robin Kirman argues that an AI tutor ready with an answer at any hour could leave teenagers less time to work through uncertainty and decide what they think.
url:https://www.theguardian.com/commenti.limit: The essay draws on developmental and clinical reasoning. It contains no comparison of teenagers who used the tutor with teenagers who went without it.

url:https://www.theguardian.com/technolo.detail: The letters describe the same exchange from opposite ends. AI can help someone put a grievance into words while the person receiving the letter still has to work out what would resolve it.
url:https://www.theguardian.com/technolo.lead: A housing investigator describes searching through long AI-written complaints to find the original problem. Another letter writer argues that people who use AI to put a grievance into words still deserve a hearing.
url:https://www.theguardian.com/technolo.limit: Individual letters give no estimate of how common this is or which complaints were justified.
